title: Rerun the one-edit study per edit kind with shuffled slots against the full meta
headline: Swapping a whole Pokemon is the one edit that clears both tests
setup: A team is six Pokemon, listed in six slots. The meta is the 50 highest-placing team files, one team listed twice. We change one thing on a team, battle the old and the new team against the meta, and see how far the win rate moves. September's battles used rules the project no longer counts, so the study ran again.
alt: Eight frames. The rerun battled every team against all 50 meta files with the six Pokemon shuffled before each battle. An edit changes one thing on one Pokemon, in one of six kinds, and each kind is tried 3 times on a team. Replays of the unchanged team show battle noise, about 3.40 points. With noise removed, one edit moves win rate by 5.90 points for a whole Pokemon swap, 4.84 for a move, 4.35 for an item, 3.66 for an ability, 1.95 for stat alignment and 1.60 for Stat Points. Only the whole Pokemon swap clears the 5-point cutoff set in the plan on 2026-09-28, and only it passes both tests, from both groups of starting teams.
terms: Edit kind

What one rule-abiding edit changes on one Pokemon: one of its four moves, its ability, the item it holds, its stat alignment, its Stat Points, or the whole Pokemon. Frame 2 shows one real edit of each kind
Stat alignment, Stat Points
Two settings of a Pokemon's numbers: which stat is raised and which lowered, and how its training points are divided among its stats
Shuffled slots
The six Pokemon get a new random order before every battle. The battle policy picks by position, so a fixed order biases scores
Replay
The same team battled 384 more times with nothing changed. Every starting team gets 3 replays
Battle noise
How far a win rate moves on a replay, by luck alone. Here a replay typically moves a score by 3.40 points
Change, in points
The typical size of the win-rate move from one edit, in percentage points, in either direction, with the typical replay move taken out
5-point cutoff
How large the change must be for an edit kind to count as beyond battle noise. Written into the plan on 2026-09-28, before any battle. The plan gives no reason for the number 5
Beyond battle noise
Test 1. A larger share of edits than of replays moves the win rate past what chance allows, and the change is at least 5 points
Rougher than Pest Control

Test 2. Pest Control is a standard optimisation benchmark where one step barely changes the score. Passing means a team's score predicts its edited neighbour's score less well than there, by correlation
Real teams outside the top 50, search-found teams
The two groups of starting teams: 24 real teams from outside the top 50, and 16 teams an earlier search produced

frames.title: 1. Why the study ran again

left.title: September study
lines: 36 of the 50 meta files as opponents

frames.takes: The rerun fixes the opponents and the slot order, and changes nothing else on purpose.
frames.measured: One thing changed by accident: the 24 real starting teams from outside the top 50 are a fresh draw, 2 shared with September, so the two runs are not paired.

frames.title: 2. The six kinds of edit, on one real team
frames.takes: An edit changes one thing on one Pokemon and leaves the other five alone.
frames.measured: These are real edits from the run. The team is Raichu, Staraptor, Garchomp, Charizard, Gholdengo and Sylveon, one of the 24 real starting teams from outside the top 50.

frames.title: 3. Three different edits of each kind
frames.takes: Each kind is tried 3 times on a team, each time with a different change, so one lucky pick cannot decide the result.
frames.measured: These are the same team's three move edits. 6 kinds times 3 edits is 18 edited teams for each starting team, and 720 across the 40 starting teams.

frames.title: 4. A replay: the same team, battled again

right.title: A replay
lines: Battle the same team 384 more times

frames.takes: A replay shows how far a score moves by luck alone. That move is battle noise.
frames.measured: The team in frame 2 scored 56.25%, then 52.3%, 53.1% and 52.9% on its 3 replays. A typical replay moves a score by 3.40 points.

frames.title: 5. From scores to a change in points

boxes.label: Edits move it
boxes.sub: 6.81 points after a whole Pokemon swap

boxes.label: Replays move it
boxes.sub: 3.40 points with no change at all

frames.takes: The change in points is the typical move after an edit, with the typical replay move taken out.
frames.measured: The two are taken apart as squares: 6.81 squared minus 3.40 squared is 5.90 squared.

frames.title: 6. Change in points for each kind, from real teams outside the top 50
frames.takes: Only the whole Pokemon swap clears the 5-point cutoff, and a move edit stops just under it.
frames.measured: From search-found teams the whole Pokemon swap is 5.85 points and a move edit 4.92.

frames.title: 7. Where the 5-point cutoff comes from

items.text: Written into the plan on 2026-09-28, before any battle was run
Kept unchanged for the rerun, so the result could not move it
The plan gives no reason for picking 5 and not 4 or 6
For scale, a replay alone moves a score by 3.40 points

frames.takes: The cutoff is a line drawn in advance for how large a change must be to count. Nobody derived the number 5.
frames.measured: A move edit misses it by 0.16 points from real teams outside the top 50 and 0.08 from search-found teams. The analysis saved no interval for that size.

frames.title: 8. Which kinds pass which test
frames.takes: One edit kind passes both tests, and three more are rougher than the benchmark from at least one group.
frames.measured: September reached this verdict too, on battles that no longer count. The change ignores direction, so a large one can be harmful.
